chapters.title: Why digital skills matter
chapters.summary: Why digital skills matter, the Essential Digital Skills Framework, and the behaviours and skills needed for hybrid working.

blocks.text: This course aims to develop the digital transformation skills for **hybrid working** as an individual or a team, rather than focusing on how digital capabilities relate to organisations. For organisations to build digital capabilities, it starts with their people having the confidence and competence to develop their skills and behaviours, so that they can make an effective contribution to the organisation.
Digital capabilities are the skills, behaviours and understanding to enable you to thrive in a digital world.
blocks.title: Digital capabilities

blocks.text: Nearly every aspect of your life relies on technology. You need the digital capabilities to use these technologies appropriately and effectively, across a range of platforms, environments and situations, in your personal life and in the workplace.

pages.title: Hybrid working and the skills employers expect

blocks.text: As the digital transformation of the workplace continues to accelerate and organisations adopt hybrid working practices, employers are focusing on the digital capabilities employees are expected to have. Key skills include:

items: communicating via email and online meeting platforms
creating documents, presentations and spreadsheets
understanding file and data management
an awareness of online security.

blocks.text: Hybrid working is where workers spend some of their time working remotely and some in the employer's workspace.
blocks.title: Hybrid working

blocks.text: This free course is part of The Open University's *Supporting hybrid working and digital transformation* collection.
After studying this course, you should be able to:

items: examine your organisation's current practices and norms around working digitally in hybrid environments (e.g. remote and onsite)
describe digital responsibility and behaviours, including GDPR, data, network security and digital wellbeing and inclusion
explore frameworks, tools and technologies for building digital capabilities
examine how organisations can take responsibility for digital sustainability
recognise that digital transformation is continuing and consider approaches for planning for digital change.

blocks.text: This first section looks at why digital skills matter, the essential skills every adult needs, and the behaviours and skills that support hybrid working.
blocks.title: In this section

blocks.text: Essential digital skills are a step towards learning lots of other new things. They can improve your confidence to use technology for work, learning and daily life. Many jobs today require digital skills. You need them even for jobs that do not ask for high levels of qualifications or experience. For example, if you work in a warehouse or a shop you may need to keep digital records of stock. You also need digital skills every day for shopping, banking, learning, and keeping in touch with family and friends.
Digital skills are not only for 'tech' jobs: they underpin everyday work and daily life.

pages.title: Video: why digital skills and capabilities matter

blocks.title: Why digital skills matter
blocks.note: Contributors share why digital skills and capabilities matter, the impact of the digital skills shortage and the digital skills organisations require. Matt Wintle (insurance business), Gemma Hallett (Fintech Wales), data specialist Nicola Askham, Dr Nick Barrett (The Open University), Sarah Jones (University of Wales Trinity Saint David) and Dr Becki Vickerstaff (Jisc) take part.

blocks.text: Key points from the video

items: Digital and data skills will be needed right across a business, but it is not 'one size fits all': understand the roles you have and what knowledge each one needs (a call-centre worker needs to understand AI and data, not build it).
Wales has acute skills shortages: around 90% of Fintech jobs are tech jobs (coders, engineers, testers), and the talent pipeline is not there yet.

The skills needed depend on the destination: a fast-growing start-up and a local authority office use very different technology; even care workers have moved from pen and paper to recording everything on an iPad.

pages.title: More from the video: data, the pandemic and everyone's role

items: **Data literacy** means reaching the same confidence with data that we have when reading words. Nearly everyone in an organisation produces or uses data, so they should recognise it as an asset and manage it as one (Nicola Askham).

When the pandemic struck, everyone discovered overnight that they needed new digital skills: running meetings in Teams, working paperless, storing and sharing content, and a new online etiquette. These are life skills that employers look for (Dr Nick Barrett).
Students must be prepared for a very digital workforce, so staff need the same levels of digital skill to teach and support them (Sarah Jones).

Almost everything, even paying car tax, is done online. Students are often assumed to be naturally digitally literate, but what matters is the *correct* use of technology. Every role, from senior leader to administrator, needs digital capability (Dr Becki Vickerstaff).

blocks.text: Digital skills for the future are essential not only to ensure organisations thrive, but also for communities and nations to protect future generations.

The Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 'A Prosperous Wales' wellbeing goal specifically focuses on the skills for the future: 'Encouraging organisations to develop a skilled population, fit for future technological change'.
blocks.title: A Prosperous Wales
Skills for the future
blocks.note: Sophie Howe, the Future Generations Commissioner for Wales, explains the skills that will be required. Work is changing exponentially; automation and AI already outperform humans at knowledge recall, so we need the human skills robots can't do - cooperation, collaboration, teamwork, empathy and critical thinking - and lifelong learning must become the new normal. There are big skills gaps in the jobs needed to meet climate targets (around 26,000 possible new green jobs in Wales in two years), and underrepresented groups must be targeted so existing inequality is not made worse.

blocks.title: Activity 2 Skills for the future
blocks.prompt: Read Section 5 of the Future Generations Commissioner's report 'A journey to a prosperous Wales' (if you can access it) and think about Sophie Howe's video on the skills that will be required for the future. How might your organisation contribute to raising the digital skills of those within it and for future generations?
blocks.model: Organisations can help by developing a skilled population that is fit for future technological change: offering digital skills training and lifelong learning opportunities to staff, building human skills such as collaboration, teamwork, empathy and critical thinking alongside technical skills, and targeting underrepresented groups so that new digital and green jobs reduce rather than widen inequality. They can also work with schools, colleges and communities to build the future talent pipeline.
points: Offer digital skills training and make lifelong learning normal.
Develop human skills such as collaboration, empathy and critical thinking.
Target underrepresented groups to avoid widening inequality.
Work with schools and communities to build skills for future generations.

blocks.text: The **Essential Digital Skills Framework** for the United Kingdom (Gov.uk, 2018) sets out the digital skills and understanding all adults require to interact in a digital world. There are five categories: communicating; handling information and content; transacting; problem solving; and being safe and legal online.

blocks.alt: Circular diagram: 'Foundation skills' at the centre, surrounded by four quarters - Communicating, Handling information and content, Transacting and Problem solving - all inside an outer ring reading 'Be safe, legal and confident online'.
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Essential Digital Skills - Framework Diagram (Crown Copyright, Gov.uk, 2018)

blocks.text: Foundation skills sit at the centre. Around them: **communicating** (communicate, collaborate and share online); **handling information and content** (find, manage and store digital information and content securely); **transacting** (apply for services, buy and sell, and manage transactions online); **problem solving** (find solutions using digital tools and online services). The outer ring surrounds them all: *be safe, legal and confident online*.

blocks.text: The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the need for both digital transformation and the ability to develop digital skills and capabilities, as individuals and organisations rapidly moved to new ways of working.

items: Reports suggest digital transformation accelerated by **about seven years** during the height of the pandemic in 2020-21.
At the first lockdowns, digital adaption (implementing remote-working solutions) was achieved in an average of **11 days** - something that pre-COVID may have taken years (McKinsey & Company, 2020).

blocks.text: This changed our ways of working and the digital capabilities we need in an unprecedented way. But the pandemic also widened the digital divide.
The digital divide is 'the gap between people who have easy access to the benefits of digital technology and those who don't' (Centre for Digital Public Services, 2022).
blocks.title: Digital divide

blocks.text: As organisations adapt to new ways of working post-pandemic, many are permanently adopting a hybrid approach, with **more than 80%** of workers suggesting they planned to work in this way (ONS, 2022).

items: Organisations need to plan for the long term and involve both their staff and external organisations to build digital skills and integrate preventive measures to reduce the digital divide.
Leaders need to develop their confidence and curiosity, and understand government and 'industry' strategies, in order to build digital capabilities that lead to effective digital transformation.

blocks.text: For higher education institutions (HEIs), it is also useful to consider students' heightened digital capabilities and expectations. Their experience has been shaped by technology use during the pandemic and by the government focus on digital skills in the curriculum. The Welsh Government's *Digital Competence Framework* for schools shows what digital skills are expected to be developed within schools.

blocks.note: Sas Amoah, a Digital Media Producer at The Open University, talks about the importance of digital skills and responsibilities. During the pandemic his team started using Teams, Zoom and online-only podcasts to capture academics and discussions for web content, and he wants to translate his skills to capturing media online effectively. Working with the public online, they follow cyber security and GDPR rules and are mindful of accessibility guidance. The digital space evolves so quickly that skills learned last year may already need updating, so he suggests organisations make digital skills training mandatory, because it is such an integral part of how people work.

chapters.title: The digital divide and inclusion
chapters.summary: The digital divide, digital inclusion for hybrid workers, and using the Jisc digital capabilities framework.

blocks.text: The digital divide is the gap between people in society who have full access to digital technologies (such as the internet and computers) and those who do not (UK Parliament, 2020).
blocks.title: Digital divide

blocks.text: In this section you will:

items: explore how the digital divide affects people's lives and work
look at the scale of digital exclusion in Wales and how organisations can support digital inclusion for hybrid workers
explore the Jisc digital capabilities framework and how institutions use it to build digital capabilities.

blocks.text: The pandemic highlighted the digital divide. During home-schooling there were frequent media reports of children without the technology to join remote lessons. Many people could not shop online due to lack of access to technology, digital capabilities or poor infrastructure - often lack of internet access.

A lack of digital skills and access can have a huge negative impact on a person's life, leading to poorer health outcomes and a lower life expectancy, increased loneliness and social isolation, less access to jobs and education. It can mean paying more for essentials, financial exclusion, an increased risk of experiencing poverty. People who are digitally excluded also lack a voice and visibility in the modern world, as government services and democracy increasingly move online. What's more, it's those already at a disadvantage - through age, education, income, disability, or unemployment - who are most likely to be missing out, further widening the social inequality gap.
The Welsh Government's report on digital inclusion and basic digital skills (gov.wales, 2020) indicates that:

items: 60,000 personal internet users (aged 16 or over) can't demonstrate the skill of using a search engine
730,000 personal internet users can't demonstrate the skills of managing privacy settings
19% of disabled people do not personally use the internet and are therefore deemed digitally excluded
76% of social housing tenants have internet access, compared to 90% of owner occupiers.

blocks.text: The *Digital inclusion and basic digital skills in Wales: 2019-2020* infographic, which summarises the Welsh Government's strategy *Digital inclusion forward look: towards a digitally confident Wales*, captures the scale of the divide. Some numbers may seem low, but those in the digital divide are often the most vulnerable, excluded from basic inclusion in society, or in areas where digital infrastructure is limited.

pages.title: Check: the scale of the divide

blocks.explain: 19% of disabled people do not personally use the internet. 76% and 90% are the internet-access figures for social housing tenants and owner occupiers.

blocks.text: The people most likely to be excluded are often those who are already most vulnerable.

pages.title: Video: digital inclusion and the digital divide (1)

blocks.title: Digital inclusion and the digital divide
blocks.note: Contributors share their insights about digital inclusion and how to narrow the digital divide: Jessica Leigh Jones, Gemma Hallett, Matt Wintle, Michael Woods, Natasha Davies and Jo Parker.

items: **Jessica Leigh Jones:** digital is a key enabler of the Well-being of Future Generations Act's goals, but it can be a double-edged sword. An SMS-based adult social care process cut waiting times, yet 12% of households in Wales lack proper broadband or mobile signal and would be excluded. Living rurally, she can't use two-factor authentication by text. Developers must think beyond what the majority can access, and FE/HE can offer short, sharp upskilling.

**Gemma Hallett:** we can't assume everyone arrives with digital skills, especially in rural Wales and areas of generational poverty. Hybrid models let Cardiff companies employ people from the valleys without travel - but if skills are missing, jobs go remote elsewhere. 99.7% of Welsh businesses are SMEs, with few resources to upskill staff.

pages.title: Video: digital inclusion and the digital divide (2)

items: **Matt Wintle:** equality for people working from home means the same opportunities and an equal working environment - through financial and technical support - rather than a two-tier system. Leave even a few people behind and a positive culture starts to break down.

**Michael Woods:** working from home needs reliable broadband, so growth may be geographically uneven. Organisations could support staff in areas with weak infrastructure, e.g. through remote hubs or communal workspaces in small towns, perhaps joined to libraries.

**Natasha Davies:** without action on different levels of digital skill we risk excluding people. Invest in basic digital skills for a good baseline, help staff and leaders to embrace new technology, and think about equality when designing meetings, collaborative spaces and socials. The Welsh Government aims for 30% of the workforce to work away from the office.

blocks.text: Jo Parker: for digital inclusion, there are three key things to think about - have you got the **kit**, have you got the **space**, have you got the **skills**? You can't make one size fit all.

pages.title: Activity 5 Research the digital divide and inclusion

blocks.text: Understanding the digital divide and approaches to closing the gap within your organisation and local community is essential. It can be overlooked when thinking about inclusion, because of an assumption that if you are working you already have the basic skills and access to infrastructure. As more people work in a hybrid way, the digital inclusion needs of remote workers may go unnoticed.

blocks.title: Activity 5 Research the digital divide and inclusion
blocks.prompt: Reflect on the video, then do your own research into the digital divide and inclusion (useful sources: the Welsh Government's 'Digital inclusion forward look: towards a digitally confident Wales', the Good Things Foundation's 'The digital divide', Digital Communities Wales, and OpenLearn's 'Inclusive education: knowing what we mean (Wales)'). Access: broadband, mobile signal and equipment (kit).
A suitable space to work at home, or hubs and communal workspaces.
Invest in basic digital skills and confidence for everyone.

pages.title: 2.1 A framework for building digital capabilities

blocks.text: Many higher education and further education institutions have adopted the **Jisc digital capabilities framework**. It expresses the essential digital skills every adult should have in the context of the workplace, and provides a means of articulating and understanding digital capabilities in an FE/HE setting. The framework states that:

At an individual level we define digital capabilities as those which equip someone to live, learn and work in a digital society. At an organisational level we need to look beyond the capabilities of individuals and consider the extent to which the culture and infrastructure of an institution enables and motivates digital practices.
The framework defines six elements at each level (Table 4).

head: Individual digital capability
Organisational digital capability
rows: Information, data and media literacies (critical use)
Digital creation, problem solving and innovation (creative production)

blocks.title: A framework for building digital capabilities
blocks.note: Dr Becki Vickerstaff, Higher Education Senior Consultant at Jisc, explains the framework. It looks at digital capability from a higher level, was developed in collaboration with the sector, and is used by many institutions nationally and internationally. Its six main areas stem off into a further 15 areas.

items: **ICT proficiency** - digital proficiency and productivity: using technologies and methods effectively.
**Information, data and media literacies** - retrieving information and knowing what to do with it.
**Digital creation, problem solving and innovation** - including digital research.
**Digital communication, collaboration and participation** - choosing the right platform to work together online, safely.
**Digital learning and development** - digital learning and digital teaching.
**Digital identity and wellbeing** - runs across the whole framework: your digital footprint, time online, staying safe, online bullying.

blocks.title: Match each description to the Jisc framework element

pairs.def: Using ICT tools, devices and software confidently, choosing the right tool for the job
Finding, evaluating and managing information, and using data to inform decisions

pairs.term: Digital creation, problem solving and innovation
pairs.def: Designing new digital materials and adopting new digital practices
Working effectively in digital teams and building digital networks
Taking part in digital learning and supporting others to teach in digital settings
Managing your digital reputation and looking after your health and work-life balance online

pages.title: One size does not fit all

blocks.text: When thinking about a digital capabilities framework, define the following so that you understand the digital skills and behaviours needed for different contexts within your HEI - one size does not fit all!

items: **People:** the group of people who need the skills
**Places:** the context in which they need to use the skills
**Technology:** the tools and systems that they need the skills to use
**Period:** the time frame in which these skills are relevant (Orlik, 2018).

blocks.q: In Orlik's (2018) four steps, what does 'Places' refer to?
options: The context in which people need to use the skills
The tools and systems people need to use
The time frame in which skills are relevant
blocks.explain: Places means the context in which the skills are used. Technology is the tools and systems; Period is the time frame.

pages.title: How the OU applies the framework

blocks.text: The Open University set Jisc's capabilities into its own context: subject experts from across the University collaborated to build and support digital capabilities through guidance, training, support and processes. 'This means that we...':

head: Capability
This means that we...
rows: use ICT tools, devices, software and services confidently, choosing the right tool for the job

blocks.title: Using the Jisc framework
blocks.note: Becki Vickerstaff recaps what the framework is, then contributors discuss how it has been used in their organisations and areas to consider for the future.

items: **Jo Parker (OU):** it lets you think about capability from an individual and an organisational perspective. The OU used it to shape its own digital and information literacy framework for students, and, for staff, to audit existing resources and build a hub that brings them together with a shared language.
**Sarah Jones (UWTSD):** the mapping 'has been done for us' - and resources such as LinkedIn Learning are already mapped to it.

**Becki Vickerstaff:** it builds consensus on what digital capability is and why it matters; institutions break it down and align it to their own provision. The pandemic accelerated digital tools and showed the need for a lifelong-learning attitude and transferable digital skills for graduates.

blocks.title: Creating the DigiCentre: how institutions use the framework
blocks.note: Becki Vickerstaff explains how the Jisc framework has been used to create digital resource areas that build the capabilities of staff and students.

items: **University of Wales Trinity Saint David:** a clear digital strategy and a dedicated hub aligned to the framework; the Discovery Tool lets individuals reflect safely on strengths and needs; embedded in induction and appraisals, with sessions for leaders, bespoke role profiles, workshops, and the LinkedIn Learning mapping.

**Edinburgh University:** mapped its own services to the framework and created a University Resource Finder to signpost staff; **student champions** acted as digital advocates training their peers; new bespoke programmes and a redesigned management and leadership course built senior buy-in.

blocks.text: Creating resources takes time - reuse good content that is already mapped to the framework.
The University of Wales Trinity Saint David worked with Jisc to create the **DigiCentre**, its one-stop shop for digital skills needs.

chapters.title: Developing your digital confidence and curiosity

pages.title: Developing your digital confidence and curiosity

blocks.text: Higher education institutions (HEIs) by their nature encourage continuous learning and being curious. They tend to have informal and formal approaches to this, often with opportunities to 'play'.
In this section you will think about how confident and curious you are with digital tools, see how one team fosters a healthy digital culture, and try two deliberately open-ended 'play' activities.
By the end of this section you should be able to:

items: explain why informal learning, play and learning from failure build digital capability
describe what a digital-first culture looks like and how reciprocal mentoring helps
reflect on how you approach an unfamiliar digital task and where you look for help

blocks.text: Building digital capabilities is not just about formal training courses on how to use the tools. It also includes **informal learning from others**, **playing with digital tools** and being **comfortable with learning from failure**.

blocks.title: Digital-first culture
blocks.text: Building a digital-first culture - where organisational leaders lead by example by focusing on people, embracing technology and having a shared vision that is communicated - encourages digital confidence and curiosity (Slack, 2022).

pages.title: Activity 10: How digitally confident are you?

blocks.text: In the original course this was a quick poll (5 minutes). Reflect on how strongly you agree with each statement:

items: *I am happy to try new things.*
*I will work out solutions.*
*I don't mind not knowing how to do something.*

blocks.title: Activity 10 How digitally confident are you?
blocks.prompt: For each of the three statements, say how much you agree and give a short example from your own digital work.
blocks.model: There is no right answer. Your responses show how comfortable you are with ambiguity. If you agree with all three, developing your digital capabilities is likely to feel like an opportunity to have fun and push limits; if you disagree, it may feel bewildering or scary - which is normal, and something you can build on by trying things out and asking for help.
points: Willingness to try new things shows digital curiosity.
Working out solutions yourself builds confidence.
Being comfortable with not knowing is part of learning.
Your comfort with ambiguity shapes how you experience digital change.

blocks.text: Depending on how comfortable you are with ambiguity and your own confidence, developing your digital capabilities (and transformation) will either be an opportunity to have fun and push the limits of what can be done, or may be bewildering and scary.

People may be afraid they will break something, do something wrong, or lose something. The latter is unlikely these days, as most organisations now use **cloud-based services**. As long as you save your work in the correct place (for example, not on your computer desktop) most things are retrievable and you can usually access previous versions.

pages.title: When things really do go wrong

blocks.text: Occasionally things do go wrong that are not fixable - and usually this is not your fault! The author's laptop simply stopped working due to a total hardware failure. However, no work or files were lost, because everything was on the servers - in the cloud - and accessible after logging onto a new laptop.

blocks.text: Learning from others is an essential part of developing your own digital capabilities. Often someone can help you use a digital tool, give you insights into the way you approach a task, or encourage you to do your own research.

If you are reimagining products, processes and systems you may have no idea what will and won't succeed. You need the confidence to develop the mindsets and expectations of stakeholders while being comfortable with stopping or adapting developments. You may need to draw on available data and input from subject matter experts to make decisions.

blocks.title: Reciprocal mentoring
blocks.text: More leaders are taking part in reciprocal mentoring - normally a junior employee mentoring someone more senior. People in the same roles can also use this approach to consider different ways of doing digital tasks and learn from each other.

Capabilities and skills vary between individuals. Don't assume that younger people are automatically experts in all types of technology: they might be competent with mobile devices and apps, but not with work tools such as Microsoft Office 365 or Google Drive. They may also lack the behavioural experience of working online in the workplace.
Have the confidence to ask questions and share your experiences within your team, or with those with specialist skills, to build collaboration and confidence.

As you become more competent and confident, share your knowledge and support others. If you are curious and not afraid to admit you don't know how to do something, most people are happy to show you. This fosters a culture of sharing and trust, and encourages people who are junior or new to contribute.

pages.title: 4.1 Case study: a healthy digital culture

blocks.text: One of the short course production teams at The Open University is an example of how to foster a healthy digital culture. Regardless of role, each member brings a different digital skill set that is of **equal importance** to delivering the product.

There is a high level of trust. Asking questions, showing others in the team how to approach tasks, and proactive behaviour are a fundamental way of working, so products can be developed quickly. Nobody assumes someone knows how to do something, and there is no mindset of 'that is someone else's job'. Everyone is flexible and helps out when required.

Authors often have never used the online platform the team delivers to. The production guidance (Table 6) focuses on the skills they already have, to build confidence, set expectations and create a safe, open environment that builds trust quickly. People are encouraged to ask for help while having access to the digital guidance and tools they need.

chapters.title: Understanding your responsibilities
chapters.summary: Your responsibilities when working digitally: wellbeing and security, governance, GDPR, IP and copyright, information security and data management.

blocks.text: When working digitally you need to understand your responsibilities and behaviours in line with your organisation's requirements and expectations. This has become more important with hybrid working: organisations now rely on trusting those working remotely to respect their requirements and to have the capability, tools and environment to do so.
In this section you will explore:

items: digital wellbeing, safety and security
digital governance and information security
the General Data Protection Regulations (GDPR)
intellectual property (IP) and copyright
information security and cyber security
data, information and digital knowledge management

blocks.text: Most HEIs have guidance and policies so staff understand the requirements for safety and security, digital governance, accessibility, inclusion and intellectual property. However, working responsibly is more wide-reaching.

Depending on your role and the products and services you deliver, there is often a set of formal and informal guidelines to consider too. These range from organisational brand guidelines and the use of systems and tools to - importantly - your **digital behaviour**: how you manage your devices and how you communicate with others.

Many organisations treat digital wellbeing, safety and security as separate, but it is useful to consider them together because they overlap: safety is inherently linked to wellbeing and security. If you do not feel 'safe' because your digital security is not sufficient, this can affect your wellbeing.

blocks.alt: Triangle diagram with 'Being digitally safe' in the centre and Wellbeing, Safety and Security at the three corners.
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Being digitally safe

pages.title: Digital life as a basic need

blocks.text: In a more digitally driven world, our reliance on technology means our digital life merits consideration as a basic need. Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs, adapted for digital life, is a useful framework for organisational and individual needs.

blocks.alt: Pyramid of Maslow 2.0 digital needs. From bottom: physiological needs (signal, phone, wifi, laptop, battery), safety needs (maps, Google, lock, email), belonging and love (Skype, Facebook, WhatsApp, Tinder), esteem (Snapchat, Twitter, Instagram), self-actualisation (Pinterest, YouTube, LinkedIn).
blocks.caption: Figure 5 Maslow 2.0: digital needs. Source: Chando (2019)

blocks.text: Similarly, the **Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015** - with its seven wellbeing goals and five ways of working - and the **Jisc Digital Wellbeing** model take a holistic approach to building digital capabilities and skills, with an emphasis on wellbeing.

This course does not cover digital wellbeing in detail. The 'Hybrid working: wellbeing and inclusion' course in the same OpenLearn collection has more on digital wellbeing and safety, and the Jisc model for digital wellbeing for individuals is also a useful resource.

blocks.model: Digital wellbeing, safety and security refer to both online and offline environments. Online: protect devices (e.g. BitLocker keys), use a strong password that complies with guidance, set up multi-factor authentication, think about how sensitive information is before sharing it, password-protect sensitive documents and know what to do with spam. Offline: secure devices when not in use, lock your computer when you leave, know who to contact if you can't get online, watch who can see your screen, what you discuss and how you store physical documents.

Some organisations have separate departments leading digital governance and information security. They ensure legal responsibilities, professional and internal standards, processes and strategies are in place, so organisations and individuals develop behaviours that give a consistent approach to operating in a digital environment.
Digital governance and information security can include:

items: GDPR (General Data Protection Regulations)
information security
data, information and digital knowledge management
intellectual property and copyright
accessibility and inclusion

communication and content

blocks.text: Many organisations use the Data Management Association (DAMA) international framework as an approach to data governance and to understanding what needs to be considered.

blocks.alt: Wheel with Data Governance at the centre surrounded by ten segments: Data Architecture, Data Modeling & Design, Data Storage & Operations, Data Security, Data Integration & Interoperability, Document & Content Management, Reference & Master Data, Data Warehousing & Business Intelligence, Metadata, Data Quality.

pages.title: Video: data governance and the wheel

blocks.title: Data governance and the DMBOK wheel - Nicola Askham, The Data Governance Coach
blocks.note: Data governance sits at the centre of the DAMA-DMBOK wheel because it provides the foundation for all other data management disciplines: roles, responsibilities, authority and processes so people make consistent decisions about data (rather than, say, starting a data-quality clean-up without understanding its impact). DAMA International publishes the DMBOK (body of knowledge) with a chapter for each discipline; each wheel segment represents one chapter and may need its own experts. Compare your organisation against the wheel: most do data security, fewer do master or reference data management - are you doing enough?

blocks.text: The wheel summarises all the data management disciplines; it helps people understand what data they have and manage it so it is good enough quality to support good decisions.

blocks.title: Data vs information
blocks.text: Data is the building blocks. A date on its own tells you nothing; in context - as part of a record showing it is someone's date of birth - it becomes **information**, and becomes valuable. People often confuse the two terms.

Data governance names roles such as a **data owner** and **data steward**, but these are few. Nicola Askham adds two roles for everyone else: a **data producer**, responsible for capturing data correctly in accordance with requirements, and a **data consumer**. Because producers and consumers are often different people, these roles help break down silos and get them talking.
AI and machine learning can give amazing insights, but they are only as good as the underlying data - so a good data governance foundation matters more than ever.

Not all organisations have a detailed digital governance framework; some have frameworks and strategy elements for 'digital activity'. A **digital governance framework** is different from a **data governance framework**, which focuses on the management of data.

A digital governance framework should go wider than data governance: it can cover GDPR, information security, data and knowledge management, IP and copyright, accessibility and inclusion, digital brands, and communication and content, supported by legal, professional and internal standards and a strategy.

blocks.title: General Data Protection Regulations
blocks.text: GDPR is a European data protection law that gives individuals more control over their personal information. For organisations, this means robust data privacy policies and processes that limit how personal data is accessed and what an organisation can do with it.
Data and information are not restricted to documents: they are content used in any system, asset or communication, digital or physical. They can exist in:

items: documents, spreadsheets, presentations
database systems
content on online learning platforms
video, audio, image assets
websites
emails
reports
staff records

blocks.text: The UK GDPR sets out seven key principles (Article 5(1); source: Information Commissioner's Office):

head: Principle
Requirement
rows: Personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to individuals.

Collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes (archiving in the public interest, scientific or historical research or statistics are not considered incompatible).
Adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes for which they are processed.
Accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date; every reasonable step must be taken to erase or rectify inaccurate data without delay.

head: Principle
Requirement
rows: Kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than necessary; longer storage only for archiving in the public interest, research or statistics, with appropriate safeguards.

Processed with appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
The controller shall be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with, these principles (Article 5(2)).

blocks.text: There may be a nominated 'controller' with oversight of GDPR, but **anyone who handles personal data** must adhere to the seven principles through the relevant organisational policies and processes. Most HEIs require annual GDPR training. Check what is in place in your organisation.

blocks.title: Match each GDPR principle to its meaning

pairs.def: Only use personal data for the specified, legitimate purposes it was collected for
Collect only what is adequate, relevant and necessary
Keep data correct and up to date; fix or erase errors without delay
Keep identifiable data no longer than necessary
Protect data against unauthorised processing, loss or damage
The controller must be able to demonstrate compliance
Process data lawfully, fairly and openly towards individuals

blocks.text: The GitLab open-source handbook offers a simple approach to help you make informed choices about sharing information - the **SAFE** framework. If any answer flags a risk, do not share without proper approvals; otherwise it is safe to share.

blocks.alt: SAFE flowchart. S: does the material include sensitive or material non-public information? Yes - stop. A: is it accurate and verifiable? No - stop. F: does it include financial data, metrics or predictions? Yes - stop. E: could sharing it have a harmful effect on team members or the business? Yes - stop; No - safe to share. Stop means do not share without proper approvals.
blocks.caption: Figure 7 GitLab SAFE framework

blocks.title: Activity 16 Think about the information and data you handle (15 minutes)
blocks.prompt: How often do you consider GDPR when you handle information and data? Are you confident your behaviour would meet the requirements of your organisation's policies and processes? Using the SAFE framework as a guide, make notes: what action, if any, do you need to take now?
blocks.model: Many people rarely think about GDPR in day-to-day work, even though data is in emails, spreadsheets, platforms and records. Checking information against SAFE - Sensitive? Accurate? Financial? Effect if shared? - before sharing helps you make informed choices. Actions might include completing GDPR training, reviewing your organisation's policies, and deleting or securing personal data you no longer need.
points: Personal data appears in many places, not just documents.
Everyone handling personal data must follow the seven principles.
Check Sensitive, Accurate, Financial and Effect before sharing.
Identify a concrete action such as training or reviewing policies.

blocks.text: When handling information and data, you also need to think about IP and copyright. It is a broad topic, but be aware of your responsibilities and your organisation's expectations.
Intellectual property normally covers:

items: the names of your products or brands
your inventions
the design or look of your products
things you write, make or produce

blocks.text: Copyright normally covers:

items: literary, dramatic, musical and artistic work
software, web content and databases
sound and music recordings
film, television and online broadcasting
published editions

blocks.text: Sources: gov.uk 'Intellectual property and your work'; adapted from the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988.

items: **Use and sharing of your organisation's information, products, services and content** - your organisation owns the IP and copyright, so be aware of what you can share in the public domain. It may be inadvisable to share details of a commercially sensitive innovation project, or an extract from a course you authored - you may not own the rights.

**Use of others' materials (third-party content)** - check the conditions of use. Some organisations, such as NASA, state them clearly; others are complicated, as the 'author' is often not the 'owner'.

blocks.title: Deeplinking
blocks.text: Deeplinking means sending users to a specific page on a website rather than its homepage. Even if articles are freely accessible, many organisations charge for deeplinking, partly because it can mean a loss of income for the site owner.
A basic rule for IP and copyright: if you are unsure, always seek advice and permission.

blocks.title: Activity 17 Explore intellectual property and copyright further (10 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Check what guidance and requirements your organisation has (for example, a Copyright Hub page like the University of Wales Trinity Saint David's). If interested, also look at gov.uk 'Patents, trade marks, copyright and designs' and the UK Copyright Service fact sheet. Note where your guidance is and one thing you learned.
blocks.model: Most HEIs provide a dedicated copyright page or library service. Find out who to ask, what you may share of your organisation's content, and how to clear third-party content before using it. When in doubt, seek advice and permission.
points: Find your organisation's copyright guidance and contact.
Your organisation usually owns IP you create at work.
Third-party content needs its conditions of use checked.
If unsure, seek advice and permission.

blocks.title: Information security
blocks.text: Information security protects the **confidentiality**, **integrity** and **availability** - the 'CIA triad' - of all assets, information and systems, whether digital or physical.

blocks.alt: Triangle with Information Security in the centre, Integrity at the top, Confidentiality bottom left and Availability bottom right.
blocks.caption: Figure 8 The CIA triad. Source: Preferred IT Group (2019)

blocks.text: Definitions based on the National Cyber Security Centre (2021b):

cards.back: Only authorised personnel, in relation to their role, should have access to information - so it is not shared or accessed without permission.
Information and data are accurate, consistent and used for their intended purpose; strong non-repudiation and authenticity controls stop data being modified or destroyed.
Information and data are readily available, with reliable access to and use of information.
Confidentiality, integrity and availability - what information security protects.

blocks.text: The primary focus is that organisations and individuals operate securely with minimal disruption, by reducing the risk of security incidents - theft of, tampering with, or deletion of information and data. Most organisations have an information security policy on using IT and digital assets safely.
Common threats (Imperva, n.d.):

items: **Poorly secured systems** - increase the risk of attacks from third parties, or misuse (intentional or unintentional) by people within the organisation.
**Social media and email attacks** - accounts are hacked, or emails trick users into an action that compromises security.
**Malware** - software that disrupts, damages, or gains unauthorised access to a computer system.

**Malware on endpoints** - the devices you use (laptops, tablets, phones) can be threatened in various ways and traditional antivirus is often not enough. Organisations can reduce risks on their own devices, but have limited control when people use their own devices for work.
**Lack of encryption** - using encryption to access devices can help prevent loss of data or corruption of equipment.

**Security misconfiguration** - all platforms and tools, including web-based tools, must be configured and updated correctly. Many updates are automatic, but some rely on individuals, who need to understand how to do them.

blocks.title: Match each security threat to its description

pairs.def: Raise the risk of third-party attacks or misuse by insiders
Hacked accounts or emails that trick users into compromising actions
Software that disrupts, damages or gains unauthorised access to a system
Threats to laptops, tablets and phones, especially personal devices
Devices accessed without protection that could prevent data loss
Tools not set up or updated correctly

blocks.title: Cyber security
blocks.text: Cyber security is how individuals and organisations reduce the risk of a cyber attack; its main focus is protecting devices and services from theft or damage. Information security protects both digital and physical information, whereas cyber security focuses only on digital protection (NCSC, n.d.).

blocks.title: Activity 18 Find out more about information security and cyber security (as long as you've got)
blocks.prompt: Investigate your organisation's approach and policy on information and cyber security. Good starting points: the ICO's information security guidance, the NCSC's 'What is Cyber Security', or the OpenLearn course 'Introduction to cyber security'. Note the key points of your organisation's policy.
blocks.model: These are complex areas. Your organisation's information security policy should explain how to use IT and digital assets safely, how confidentiality, integrity and availability are protected, and what you must do - such as keeping devices updated, using encryption and reporting incidents.
points: Find and read your organisation's information security policy.
Information security covers digital and physical; cyber security digital only.
Note your own duties, e.g. updates, encryption, reporting.
Use trusted sources such as the ICO and NCSC.

blocks.text: As well as securing systems, we must think about the security of the information we hold, how we protect it and how we share it. Information is normally classified as **unclassified**, **internal** or **confidential** (part of Information Classification Software for ISO 27001). Understand your responsibilities for each.

head: Class
Description and examples
rows: Not particularly valuable; no requirement to protect it. Anyone can access it for any purpose, including release to the public or clients - e.g. press releases, job vacancies.
Has value internally and may have some value to competitors. May be distributed freely within the organisation - e.g. internal memos, employment data, contract information.
Significant value; there may be legal requirements to protect it. Access limited to designated roles or tiers - e.g. intellectual property, customer payment details, long-term strategic planning.

blocks.text: Source: IT Governance (n.d.)

blocks.q: How should a set of customer payment details be classified?
blocks.explain: Customer payment details have significant value and legal protection requirements, so access is limited to designated roles: confidential.

blocks.text: Information has value, so you need to understand digital knowledge management.

blocks.title: Digital knowledge management
blocks.text: Digital knowledge management is the process for identifying, capturing, organising, storing and sharing digital information effectively so that it is easily accessible for all those who require access. The right **metadata** (data about the data) lets computer-automated tools access - or search - the assets.

blocks.title: Managing data - Nicola Askham, The Data Governance Coach
blocks.note: Data is the lifeblood of every organisation. Poorly managed data leads to bad decisions: clients made catastrophic decisions because they trusted reports with incorrect data. COVID made organisations raise their data management game and showed the need to document your understanding of data, since remote workers can no longer just ask a neighbour. Building a data culture remotely is harder, so a formal communications and training plan is needed, with different messages for senior leaders and for junior staff entering data. Bad data harms customer and student experience (e.g. poor timetabling data), and digital transformation always requires well-managed data - ideally with data governance in place before it starts.

items: Decisions based on poorly managed data can be to the detriment of the organisation, even when people act in good faith.
Hybrid working makes documenting what data means, and whether you may use it, more important.
Data governance is largely a culture and mindset change: data is an asset - so plan communication and training rather than leaving it to chance.
Digital transformation programmes automate and speed up processes - and they always require data that is managed well.

blocks.text: In an ideal world you would start data governance before a digital transformation programme; if not, do it as part of the programme, because it won't succeed without it (Nicola Askham).

Digital Knowledge Management (DKM) is a key digital capability integrated throughout the Jisc Digital Capabilities framework. Increasingly it covers how your organisation's digital tools and systems are connected and 'talk' to each other, and how they are used.
Specialists design workflows, develop technology and produce policies, but **everyone** needs to understand the behaviour required to manage knowledge effectively. At a basic level:

items: save files to the correct location
don't keep files on your own hard drives
back up files regularly
don't duplicate copies of files or save them in more than one place
add correct file names and metadata

blocks.text: Managing your digital world effectively is probably the most useful digital capability you can learn: growing collaboration tools and machine learning demand better DKM.

blocks.title: Managing media data - Jonathan Morgan, CEO, Object Matrix Ltd
blocks.note: Object Matrix (Cardiff) makes data storage for the media industry. Asset management is, at its core, search - finding the right video among thousands of hours, possibly helped by AI. The cloud is 'someone else's computer': public, private, on-premises or hybrid. Key concerns when managing data: reduce time spent managing it, security (hacks, hardware failure), and usability with other applications. Governance means rules on who can access, read, change or delete data, and auditing. Remote working raises new risks: who in the household can see the material, is it left lying around? Media has leaked through home working and hacks, including ransomware.

blocks.title: Activity 19 How do you manage digital media assets? (20 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Many HEIs now create more audio and video. Consider how your organisation manages digital media assets, then familiarise yourself with its policies and guidance for managing data. Make notes.
blocks.model: Good practice includes storing assets in a managed, secure, searchable place with good metadata; clear governance on who can access, change or delete them, with auditing; and extra care when working from home - who can see the material and where it is kept.
points: Assets should be stored centrally and be searchable with metadata.
Governance sets who can access, change or delete assets.
Security protects against hacks, leaks and hardware failure.
Remote working needs extra care with who can see material.

blocks.title: Zero trust
blocks.text: A zero-trust approach assumes the environments data is accessed from (e.g. home Wi-Fi and devices) cannot be fully trusted. Instead of trying to secure everything, you firewall and sandbox where the data is kept and control very tightly, at a granular level, what can access it.

Jonathan Morgan describes a multinational post-production house that was badly hacked: once through the firewall, attackers reached every system, even planting hacks in firmware. The only systems not compromised were those with zero trust, which had their own firewall and didn't trust other computers on the same network.

He also notes that the pandemic transferred a huge amount of trust from management to the workforce - and in the main, staff responded by delivering the same quality and quantity of work as in the office.

blocks.title: Try it: protect information at work
blocks.intro: Classify workplace information, decide what to do in realistic scenarios (CIA triad, GDPR, threats, IP, SAFE, zero trust, wellbeing) and build your own security checklist from Table 7.

blocks.text: Working digitally and hybrid means understanding and acting on your responsibilities:

items: Wellbeing, safety and security overlap - consider them together, online and offline.
Digital governance covers GDPR, security, data and knowledge management, IP, accessibility, brand and content; data governance sits at the centre of the DAMA wheel.
Anyone handling personal data must follow the seven GDPR principles.
If unsure about IP or copyright, seek advice and permission.
Information security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability; cyber security focuses on digital protection.
Classify information and manage files well - DKM is everyone's job.

blocks.q: Only the nominated GDPR controller has a responsibility to follow the seven GDPR principles.
blocks.explain: Anyone who handles personal data must adhere to the seven principles through organisational policies and processes.

blocks.q: What does the 'I' in the CIA triad stand for?
blocks.explain: The CIA triad is confidentiality, integrity and availability.

blocks.q: What is the key difference between information security and cyber security?
options: Cyber security protects physical documents only
Information security protects digital and physical information; cyber security only digital
Information security is only about passwords
blocks.explain: Information security covers both digital and physical information, whereas cyber security focuses only on digital protection.

blocks.q: Which of these is NOT one of the basic DKM behaviours listed in the course?
options: Saving files to the correct location
Keeping copies of files on your own hard drive
Adding correct file names and metadata
blocks.explain: You should not keep files on your own hard drives or duplicate them in more than one place.

blocks.q: In the SAFE framework, which answer means you should NOT share without approvals?
options: The information is accurate and verifiable
The material contains no sensitive information
The information includes financial data, metrics or predictions
Sharing it would have no harmful effect
blocks.explain: Financial data, metrics or predictions (F) mean stop: do not share without proper approvals.

blocks.q: Why do many site owners charge for deeplinking?
options: It can lead to a loss of income for the site owner
It breaks copyright law in all cases
blocks.explain: Deeplinking sends users to a specific page rather than the homepage, which can lead to a loss of income for the site owner.

blocks.q: Which item sits at the centre of the DAMA-DMBOK wheel?
blocks.explain: Data governance is at the centre because it provides the foundation for all other data management disciplines.

chapters.title: Digital futures: digital transformation
chapters.summary: What digital transformation means, what drives it, the three Ds, and reducing your digital carbon footprint - plus the course conclusion.

blocks.text: Digital transformation accelerated during the pandemic, and it will keep going. In this final section you look at what digital transformation means, what is driving it, how higher education institutions (HEIs) might approach it, and how to reduce your digital carbon footprint.
By the end of this section you should be able to:

items: define digital transformation and name key themes organisations are considering
explain what 'Industry 4.0' means today
distinguish digitization, digitalization and digital transformation
describe the causes of digital carbon emissions and actions you can take to reduce them

blocks.text: According to a new McKinsey Global Survey of executives, their companies have accelerated the digitization of their customer and supply-chain interactions and of their internal operations by three to four years. And the share of digital or digitally enabled products in their portfolios has accelerated by a shocking seven years.
blocks.by: McKinsey & Company (2020), COVID-19 digital transformation & technology

blocks.title: Digital transformation
blocks.text: Digital transformation is how organisations implement business models that consider and leverage the development of technology. It aims to enhance the capability of its people and develop processes to ensure it can succeed in the future.

The rapid acceleration saw companies introduce temporary solutions that are now embedded and evolving to meet new ways of working. Organisations and individuals will need the resilience to keep working with uncertainty and learn new skills as new technology is adopted.
Key themes organisations are considering:

items: automation of business processes - machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI)
cloud computing
use of data to drive decision making
attracting talent with the right digital capabilities
zero-trust approach to security
how the metaverse will develop
sustainability - reaching net-zero, and carbon footprints

blocks.title: Digital transformation and the capabilities needed for the future
blocks.note: Contributors explain what organisations need to consider for digital transformation. Jessica Leigh Jones: 'digital' now means workflow, leadership and agile ways of working; don't mandate tools - the tool is part of the workflow, not a substitute for it. Gemma Hallett: workplaces differ hugely, from start-ups to councils and the care sector, where moving from pen and paper to iPads has exposed big skill gaps. Jonathan Morgan: customers want rounded, fully working, documented products. Becki Vickerstaff: everything is online now; don't assume students are naturally digitally literate - embed lifelong learning. Myles Ogilvie: every organisation is enabled by software. Natasha Davies: invest in basic skills and a culture of constant learning. Elise Lockyer: the best skill is the desire to keep learning and stay curious.

blocks.title: Three digital roles
blocks.text: Jessica Leigh Jones describes three types of digital role: **digital architects/leaders**, who understand digital workflows and facilitate collaboration; **digital developers** - coders and programmers who build the tools; and **digital consumers** - everybody else, who all need basic-level digital consumer skills.

items: **Gemma Hallett:** technology varies enormously - from fast-growing start-ups to councils using big desktop monitors. In domestic care, workers moved from pen and paper to tablet apps, and the digital skills shortage there is huge.

**Jonathan Morgan:** in education it's easy to play with a concept, but in the real world customers want a 100% working product, with documentation. New tools - such as searching video by faces, text or type of scene - will transform how media data is used.

**Becki Vickerstaff:** even paying car tax is online. There's a belief that students arrive naturally digitally literate, but that isn't necessarily true; they need transferable digital skills, and we need to embed lifelong learning.

**Myles Ogilvie:** the pandemic showed every organisation is enabled by software - 'software is eating the world'. Unlike mass production, users don't know what they need until they see it. Leaders should get clarity on purpose, organise for the flow of value rather than role-based silos, and keep re-prioritising based on lessons learned. There is no finite end point.

**Natasha Davies:** invest in basic digital skills for everyone, then support people to embrace new technology through a culture where constant learning is the norm. Leaders must understand how tools support agile, inclusive working and lead by example.
**Elise Lockyer:** nobody can predict the next 5-10 years; the best skill is the desire to constantly learn, ask questions, stay curious and evolve.

blocks.title: Match each contributor to their key point

pairs.def: The tool doesn't compensate for the workflow - it is part of it
Care workers moving from pen and paper to tablets face a big skills gap
Customers want a rounded, fully working, documented product
Don't assume students arrive naturally digitally literate
Every organisation is enabled by software
The best skill is the desire to keep learning and stay curious

blocks.text: We frequently hear the term 'the 4th Industrial Revolution'. Jessica Leigh Jones MBE, CEO of iungo Solutions, briefly explains what it means.

blocks.title: Industry 4.0 - Jessica Leigh Jones MBE
blocks.note: Industry 4.0 originated in German manufacturing and describes the fourth industrial revolution: bringing technologies together to increase productivity, efficiency and quality. Its meaning has broadened across almost every industry to mean digital transformation - less about technology (though robots and process automation are part of it) and more about an evolution in human behaviour, such as consumers' expectation of immediate service.

blocks.title: Industry 4.0
blocks.text: Today Industry 4.0 means: which techniques, technologies, tools and ways of working can we adopt to meet the needs of the modern consumer?

blocks.alt: Poster titled '20 ways to achieve digital transformation': 20 numbered boxes in four rows labelled Mindset, People, Process and Tools.
blocks.caption: Figure 9 20 ways to achieve digital transformation. Source: The New Reality (n.d.)

blocks.title: Activity 20 What is driving digital transformation? (15 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Read 'The 5 great shifts driving digital transformation' (digileaders.com) and The New Reality group's research themes. Then use the '20 ways' infographic to think about what is needed to enable digital transformation in your organisation. Which steps seem most appropriate or relevant in your context, and why?
blocks.model: Answers will vary. Many HEIs might pick mindset steps such as starting with the core mission and being transparent; people steps such as breaking down silos and getting good data people; process steps such as co-designing with your audience and stopping what isn't working; and tool steps such as going cloud-based and making sure it is sustainable.
points: Choose specific steps from the 20 ways.
Cover mindset, people, process and tools.
Relate the steps to your own organisation's context.
Explain why those steps matter most.

head: Row
Steps
rows: 1 Start with the core mission; 2 Fully commit and accept the pain; 3 Show don't tell; 4 Be transparent; 5 Think broader than web and social
6 Find someone to guide you; 7 Sack the 'no' person; 8 Replace trustees; 9 Break down silos; 10 Get some good data people
11 Keep your horizons short; 12 Find ways to innovate; 13 Co-design with your audience; 14 Collaborate and partner; 15 If it isn't working stop doing it
16 Assume it already exists; 17 Go cloud-based; 18 Modular not one size fits all; 19 Track live performance; 20 Make sure it's sustainable

blocks.text: EDUCAUSE suggests three Ds (Reinitz, 2020) as stages on the journey:

blocks.alt: Rising arrow with five stages: 1 Digitize information and 2 Organize information (Digitization); 3 Automate processes and 4 Streamline processes (Digitalization); 5 Transform the institution (Digital transformation).
blocks.caption: Figure 10 Digital transformation

head: Stage
Meaning
rows: Changing from analogue or physical to digital form: digitize and organize information.
Using digital technologies and information to transform individual institutional operations: automate and streamline processes.

A series of deep and coordinated culture, workforce and technology shifts that enable new educational and operating models and transform an institution's operations, strategic directions and value proposition.

blocks.title: Activity 21 Explore what digital transformation for HEIs might involve (15 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Explore 'Leading the digital transformation of higher education' (Times Higher Education), 'Dx: Digital Transformation of Higher Education' and 'Consider the Three Ds When Talking about Digital Transformation' (EDUCAUSE). Using the three Ds, where do you feel your HEI is in its journey to digital transformation? Give examples.
blocks.model: Many HEIs have largely digitized information and are digitalizing - automating and streamlining individual processes such as enrolment or assessment. Full digital transformation requires deep, coordinated culture, workforce and technology shifts that change the institution's operating model, strategy and value proposition.
points: Place your HEI at digitization, digitalization or transformation.
Give an example as evidence.
Transformation needs coordinated culture, workforce and technology shifts.
Note what would move your HEI to the next stage.

blocks.text: Digital transformation must be considered in the wider context of organisational development and your operating environment - including reducing carbon emissions to reach net-zero by 2050.

blocks.q: An HEI automates and streamlines its assessment process using digital tools. Which of the three Ds is this?
blocks.explain: Using digital technologies to transform individual institutional operations (automating and streamlining processes) is digitalization.

blocks.text: Sustainability is now essential and part of the digital transformation organisations must consider. This section looks at what HEIs can do to manage their carbon footprint.
IT is often one of the biggest contributors to an education institution's own carbon footprint, with one UK college attributing 20% of its emissions to IT alone.

Reducing digital carbon footprints, of organisations and individuals, will become a priority as HEIs have committed to net zero by 2050 or before. Jisc's report focuses on the source and impact of four key areas: **procurement**, **on-premises IT**, **cloud technologies** and **remote working**.

blocks.title: Exploring digital carbon footprints - Scott Stonham, report author
blocks.note: Scott outlines the report's four areas. Procurement: about 80% of IT's carbon emissions are 'embodied' - generated manufacturing, building and distributing equipment - plus e-waste; only around 20% comes from use. So buy wisely, extend equipment life (refurbished and remanufactured IT) and avoid landfill. Scope 3 emissions (15 categories) are the lion's share for all organisations, and purchased goods and services are 70-90% of most scope 3. On-premises IT now stretches into smart buildings. Cloud is 'out of sight, out of mind', but storing, accessing and processing data has a carbon cost; switch off unneeded cloud apps and use providers' carbon dashboards. Remote working: understand staff energy use and avoid unnecessary travel, e.g. for replacement equipment.

blocks.title: Embodied carbon
blocks.text: Most of IT's carbon footprint (around 80%) is embodied in manufacturing and distributing equipment, so the biggest lever is wiser, longer-term purchasing and longer product lifetimes.
Articles on OpenLearn by Scott Stonham:

items: Reducing the digital carbon footprint of the cloud
Reducing the carbon footprint of on-premises IT
How we can all tackle our digital carbon footprints
Reducing digital carbon footprint through responsible procurement
Digital carbon footprints and remote working
How can corporations reduce digital carbon footprints
What is a digital carbon footprint?

blocks.text: Strategy for reducing your digital carbon footprint must be considered alongside all elements of organisational development - see the 'Hybrid working: Organisational development' course in this collection. As organisations adopt more sustainable practices, you need to be open to new ways of working and commit to changes in your professional and personal life.
Digital carbon emissions are hard to visualise - how often do you think about what is involved for technology to exist? When you talk about cloud computing, what image comes to mind?
At a basic level, the rising digital carbon footprint is caused by:

items: manufacturing and shipping of parts and products
powering and cooling of technology infrastructures
disposal of electronic waste (e-waste)
behaviour of consumers

blocks.text: Manufacturing is not always sustainable; data centres - the cloud, the physical servers that store and process data - consume energy continually and need cooling ventilation; devices need energy to run; and e-waste is hard to recycle because of the non-renewable resources in products.

blocks.title: Digital data and carbon - Scott Stonham
blocks.note: To change behaviour we must measure, communicate and reward. First set a baseline, then reward improvement against it. Digital is not carbon-free: Stanford University estimated storing 100 GB of data generates about 0.2 tons of carbon emissions a year, and Jisc research suggests 90% of data is generated, stored and never used again. Measure how much unused data people hold and make deleting it easy - more than two or three steps and people won't do it. Other targets: sending huge documents and emails, reply-all, and video calls - turning video off for even five minutes of a one-hour call makes a difference.

blocks.title: Activity 22 Reducing your digital data carbon footprint (10 minutes)
blocks.prompt: Organisations' digital data grows daily; policies and automated systems help, but some reduction depends on individuals. As you watch, note areas that could easily be adopted, and commit to changes you can make as an individual.
blocks.model: Easy wins include deleting data and emails you no longer need, avoiding sending large attachments and reply-all, and turning video off for part of long calls. Organisations can measure data use, set a baseline, communicate simple steps and reward improvement.
points: Digital is not carbon-free - stored data has a footprint.
Much stored data is never used again, so delete what you don't need.
Make changes simple: two or three steps.
Measure, communicate and reward against a baseline.
Commit to specific personal changes.

pages.title: Simple tips to cut your footprint

blocks.text: Tips from the Exploring Digital Carbon report:

items: Consider how much you use your smartphone (average usage is 2.5 hours a day).
Reduce the brightness of your monitor.
Turn off devices, even in 'stand-by mode'.
Reduce the use of email - see 'The hidden cost of your emails on the planet'.
Simplify email signatures - remove unnecessary images.
Delete electronic files and emails you no longer need and empty your deleted items folders.
Download instead of stream audio and video.
Unsubscribe from e-newsletters you no longer want.
Extend the life of your products - think of the four Rs: reduce, repair, reuse, recycle.

blocks.title: Tips for reducing your digital carbon footprint - Scott Stonham
blocks.note: Standby still draws power: a large TV about 0.7 watts and a smart speaker up to 3.8 watts, 24 hours a day - so turn off rather than standby. Turn things down: reducing a 4K monitor from its default 95% to 55% brightness saves about 10 watts every hour with no difference in use. Dark mode on OLED screens switches black pixels off, giving almost 30% more phone battery life. Even though 80% of emissions come from what we buy, these habits matter preventatively: as our digital use accelerates, energy in use could become the biggest factor.

blocks.q: Because most IT emissions come from manufacturing, individual habits like lowering screen brightness make no meaningful difference.
blocks.explain: Scott argues small changes multiplied across thousands of people add up, and building awareness now prevents a 'runaway scenario' as digital use grows.

blocks.text: Developing digital skills, capabilities and behaviours, as an individual and as an organisation, is a continual process as technology and ways of working evolve. Our reliance on technology is essential to live and work.

As your confidence and competence grow you will be able to make more informed decisions and use technology responsibly and sustainably to your advantage - so that your organisation's needs, and those of your employees, students and the wider community, can be met in a digital world.

At the start of the course you were asked to read 'A journey to a prosperous Wales' - Section 5, Skills for the future. Wales is considered one of the most advanced countries in the world for its innovative approach to sustainability through the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015, and its digital strategy sets out what is needed to develop skills and infrastructure for the future.

blocks.prompt: Drawing on your notes from the course and the Digital Strategy for Wales, reflect: what do HEIs need to focus on for the future to build digital capabilities and ensure their digital transformation supports the wellbeing of future generations?
blocks.model: HEIs could focus on basic and advanced digital skills for all staff and students, a culture of confidence, curiosity and continuous learning, responsible behaviour (security, GDPR, data and knowledge management), inclusion so nobody is left behind, and sustainable digital practice that reduces carbon footprints - all aligned with wellbeing goals.
points: Build digital capabilities and skills for everyone.
Foster confidence, curiosity and lifelong learning.
Work responsibly: security, data protection and governance.
Make digital transformation inclusive and sustainable.
Link transformation to the wellbeing of future generations.

items: Digital transformation means implementing business models that leverage technology, building people's capability and processes for the future.
Key themes include AI and automation, cloud, data-driven decisions, digital talent, zero trust, the metaverse and sustainability.
Industry 4.0 is now less about technology and more about changing human and consumer behaviour.
The three Ds: digitization, digitalization, digital transformation.
About 80% of IT emissions are embodied; buy wisely, extend product life, and cut data, standby and brightness.

blocks.q: According to McKinsey, by how much did the share of digital or digitally enabled products accelerate during the pandemic?
blocks.explain: Digitisation of interactions and operations accelerated by three to four years; the share of digital products by a 'shocking seven years'.

blocks.q: Which of the following are key future themes organisations are considering? (Select all that apply.)
options: Use of data to drive decision making
blocks.explain: Paper-based processes are not a theme; zero trust, data-driven decisions and sustainability are.

blocks.q: Roughly what share of IT's carbon emissions is 'embodied' in manufacturing, building and distributing equipment?
blocks.explain: Scott Stonham explains about 80% is embodied carbon, and around 20% comes from use.

blocks.q: In Jessica Leigh Jones's three digital roles, who are 'digital consumers'?
options: Everybody else, who all need basic digital consumer skills
blocks.explain: Architects/leaders and developers are specialist roles; everyone else is a digital consumer needing basic-level skills.

blocks.q: Which tip is recommended to reduce your digital carbon footprint?
options: Stream audio and video instead of downloading
Simplify email signatures by removing unnecessary images
blocks.explain: The report recommends downloading rather than streaming, turning devices off, simplifying signatures and extending product life.

blocks.q: Storing data in the cloud has no carbon footprint because it is 'out of sight'.
blocks.explain: Storing, accessing and processing data in the cloud has a carbon cost - digital is not carbon-free.
